[Page 1]

THE STRANGE CASE
OF
DR. JEKYLL AND MR. HYDE

By Robert Louis Stevenson

First Edition

London: Longmans, Green, and Co. 1886

[Page 2]

STORY OF THE DOOR

Mr. Utterson the lawyer was a man of a rugged countenance, that was never lighted by a smile; cold, scanty and embarrassed in discourse; backward in sentiment; lean, long, dusty, dreary, and yet somehow lovable. At friendly meetings, and when the wine was to his taste, something eminently human beaconed from his eye; something indeed which never found its way into his talk, but which spoke not only in these silent symbols of the after-dinner face, but more often and loudly in the acts of his life. He was austere with himself; drank gin when he was alone, to mortify a taste for vintages; and though he enjoyed the theatre, had not crossed the doors of one for twenty years. But he had an approved tolerance for others; sometimes wondering, almost with envy, at the high pressure of spirits involved in their misdeeds; and in any extremity inclined to help rather than to reprove.

"I incline to Cain's heresy," he used to say quaintly: "I let my brother go to the devil in his own way." In this character, it was frequently his fortune to be the last reputable acquaintance and the last good influence in the lives of down-going men. And to such as these, so long as they came about his chambers, he never marked a shade of change in his demeanour.

No doubt the feat was easy to Mr. Utterson; for he was undemonstrative at the best, and even his friendship seemed to be founded in a similar catholicity of good nature. It is the mark of a modest man to accept his friendly circle ready-made from the hands of opportunity; and that was the lawyer's way. It came not only from his own circle, but from the entire district that he received the title of Judge. It was an epithet that pleased him greatly, and he bore it as a soldier bears a decoration.

[Page 3]

SEARCH FOR MR. HYDE

That evening Mr. Utterson came home to his bachelor house in sombre spirits and sat down to dinner without relish. It was his custom of a Sunday, when this meal was over, to sit close by the fire, a volume of some dry divinity on his reading-desk, until the clock of the neighbouring church rang out the hour of twelve, when he would go soberly and gratefully to bed. On this night, however, as soon as the cloth was taken away, he would take his candle and go upstairs to his business room; there he would open his safe, take from the most private part of it a document endorsed on the envelope as Dr. Jekyll's Will, and sitting down by the light of a candle, would read it through carefully. The will was holograph, for Mr. Utterson, though he took charge of it, had refused to lend the least assistance in making it.

The document ran as follows: 'I, Henry Jekyll, M.D., D.C.L., LL.D., F.R.S., &c., &c., being of sound mind and body, do hereby declare that all my worldly goods, possessions, and estate, both real and personal, I hereby bequeath, devise, and bequeath unto my dear friend and benefactor Edward Hyde, Esq., also known as Mr. Edward Hyde, his heirs and assigns, in fee simple, forever, to have and to hold, use and enjoy, and dispose of as he shall see fit, without any condition, limitation, or restriction whatsoever, and I do hereby request, direct, and enjoin that all my said property, both real and personal, shall be delivered to the said Edward Hyde, his heirs and assigns, immediately upon my death or disappearance, and that no inquiry or investigation shall be made into the circumstances of my death or disappearance.'

The lawyer stared at the document with an expression of mingled astonishment and horror. He had always regarded the clause as a singular feature of the will, and had more than once attempted to have it altered. But Jekyll had resisted all his entreaties with a strange obstinacy. 'I cannot do without him,' was his invariable reply. 'I have an interest in him.' And now, after many years, the clause had borne fruit at last.

[Page 4]

It was two o'clock when Utterson found himself standing before the door of the humble house in which Mr. Hyde dwelt. The building was of no great pretensions; a two-story brick building, with a plain front, and but one window on each floor, looking out on the street. The door was of oak, studded with iron nails, and had a brass knocker. The lawyer knocked; there was no reply. He knocked again, more loudly; still no reply. He tried the handle; the door was unlocked, and he entered.

The room within was bare and mean; a deal table, a few chairs, a chest of drawers, and on the mantelpiece a clock. But the place was dismantled as if for a removal. Boxes and trunks were standing about, some open, some closed; and in one corner a pile of books and papers lay heaped together, as if hastily gathered. The whole aspect of the room suggested flight and haste.

Mr. Utterson's nerves, at this unseasonable hour, and in this strange place, were already somewhat shaken, and what he now saw did not tend to reassure him. The furniture was in keeping with the room: cheap, commonplace, and somewhat sordid. On the walls were a few cheap prints, and a looking-glass. But the lawyer's attention was arrested by something lying on the floor beside one of the open trunks. It was a stick; and Utterson recognized it as one that he had himself presented to Henry Jekyll many years before.

He took it up and examined it. It was of a handsome wood, and had a mount of silver. In the handle, under a little sliding cover, there was a pocket for a few cards. Utterson opened this and found within, among other trifles, a cheque-book, and the cheque-book was filled with blanks. This circumstance, taken in connection with the dismantled appearance of the room and the evident haste of departure, suggested to the lawyer that Mr. Hyde had left under pressure of some sudden alarm.

[Page 5]

DR. JEKYLL WAS QUITE AT EASE

The week after, was one of the finest of the winter; and in the clear, dry air, under the white sunshine, the doctor walked with a lighter step than he had been used to for many months. He seemed to have regained his old self; and the neighbourhood, which had been so much alarmed by his former habits, began to breathe more freely. But there was still a cloud upon his mind, and for many days he avoided the neighbourhood of the court, where his late adventure had occurred.

In a kind of desperate loyalty to his friend, Mr. Utterson, as soon as the news reached him that the doctor was better, hastened to call. The servant, who answered the door, told him that the doctor was out. 'Then I will wait,' said the lawyer; and he was shown into the consulting-room. He had been there but a few minutes when the doctor entered, and with a cordial greeting, shook hands with his visitor.

But Mr. Utterson's interest in his friend was not yet satisfied. He had seen the change that had come over Jekyll; the pallor, the emaciation, the strange and sudden fluctuations of his temper; and he was determined to get to the bottom of the matter. He was a man of strong determination, and when he once set his mind upon a thing, he was not easily turned aside. And now, with the new light that had been thrown upon the mystery by the revelations of the night, he was more than ever resolved to unravel the web of circumstances that surrounded his friend.

The doctor, on his part, seemed to welcome the visit. He was in good spirits, and talked freely of various subjects, though he carefully avoided any reference to Hyde or to the will. Mr. Utterson noticed this reticence, but did not press the matter. He knew that the doctor was a man of few words, and that it was better to let him take his own time in opening up on a subject that was evidently painful to him.

[Page 6]

THE LAST NIGHT

On the ninth of January, the weather being very bitter, Mr. Utterson sat by his fireside one evening, after dinner, with a glass of wine beside him. The lamp had not yet been brought in, and the room was lighted only by the fire. The lawyer was thinking of the strange events of the past few weeks, and especially of the disappearance of Hyde, which had caused so much alarm in the neighbourhood. He was also thinking of the will, and of the clause that bequeathed everything to Hyde, and of his many attempts to persuade Jekyll to alter it.

As he sat thus, the door of his room was thrown open, and Poole, the doctor's servant, entered. The man was pale and trembling, and his appearance plainly showed that he had been greatly agitated. 'Mr. Utterson, sir,' he said, 'I am very glad to see you. I have been trying to find you all day. Something is the matter with my master. I am afraid something has happened to him.'

The lawyer rose hastily. 'What do you mean, Poole?' he asked. 'What has happened? Tell me at once.' But the servant was too agitated to speak clearly. He could only repeat that something was wrong, and that the master had shut himself up in his cabinet, and would not answer to any call. 'It is not the first time, sir,' he added, 'that I have seen him thus. But this time it is different. I have a great fear that some harm has come to him.'

Mr. Utterson lost no time in putting on his coat and hat, and accompanying Poole to the doctor's house. The night was cold and dark, and the streets were deserted. The two men walked rapidly through the silent city, neither speaking a word, for each was occupied with his own thoughts and fears. When they reached the house, Poole led the way to the back entrance, and they entered by a passage that led to the laboratory. The door of the laboratory was locked; but Poole had a key, and they entered.
The laboratory was a large room, fitted up with chemical apparatus of various kinds, and lit by a gas lamp that hung from the ceiling. In the centre of the room stood a table, on which were various bottles and jars, and a glass case containing some instruments. At one end of the room was a door, covered with a green baize, which led to the cabinet where the doctor usually worked. It was towards this door that Poole now pointed with a trembling hand. 'That is the door, sir,' he whispered; 'that is the door into the cabinet. And it is from behind that door that the voice comes. It is not my master's voice. I have served him many years, and I know his voice as well as I know my own. But this is not his voice.' The lawyer listened, but could hear nothing. The house was perfectly still. 'Are you sure, Poole?' he asked. 'I am sure, sir,' was the reply. 'I have heard it several times. It is a strange voice, and it cries for help. But it will not open the door.' Mr. Utterson approached the green door and listened. For a moment there was silence; then, from within, there came a sound that made his blood run cold. It was a voice, indeed, but so changed, so unnatural, so full of anguish and despair, that it seemed to belong to another world. 'For God's sake, have mercy!' cried the voice. 'Have mercy!' The lawyer and the servant looked at each other in horror. 'What shall we do?' whispered Poole. 'We must break down the door,' said Utterson, with a determined look. And, seizing a heavy axe that stood near the fireplace, he approached the door.

[Page 8]

They paused a moment, looking at each other, with the same question in their eyes. Then, with a simultaneous effort, they dashed the door open. The cabinet was empty. But in the centre of the floor there lay a man, writhing in agony. He was dressed in clothes that were too large for him, and his face was convulsed with pain. It was Hyde. But as they watched, the convulsions ceased, the features changed, and the figure before them became that of Dr. Jekyll. The doctor was dead. In his hand he held a letter, addressed to Mr. Utterson. The lawyer took it with a trembling hand and opened it. It contained a brief confession, in which Jekyll told the whole story of his double life, and of the drug that had enabled him to change his personality at will. The letter ended with these words: 'I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end.'
